title: Stop Trying to Make Everyone Successful
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham builds this leadership essay around a single metaphor from her friend Toyin Ajayi (CEO of Cityblock Health): the difference between hosting a dinner party and hosting a potluck. A dinner party host is responsible for every detail and personally ensures each guest has a great time -- the trap many early managers fall into, measuring their own success by whether every report succeeds. A potluck host picks a good spot, brings the tables, invites the right people, and gets out of the way. Graham's argument is that management is fundamentally potluck work -- creating the right conditions -- not dinner party work (personally engineering each person's success). She applies the Waterline Model diagnostic: before attributing failure to individuals, managers must audit structural conditions -- role clarity, expectation clarity, goal clarity, team dynamics -- because most underperformance traces to broken environments, not broken people. The article also addresses the flip side: once conditions are genuinely sound, persistent contortion to make someone succeed (repeated same feedback, routing work around them, tiptoeing in 1-on-1s) is itself bad management that harms the team. The potluck metaphor then extends to building communities, products, and any domain where someone sets up conditions others opt into.
points: The core reframe: management is potluck work (create conditions, clear the beehives, bring the tables) not dinner party work (personally ensure each guest has a great time) -- and confusing the two is the most common failure mode of early managers.

The Waterline Model diagnostic: before attributing underperformance to individuals, managers must audit structural conditions -- role clarity, expectation clarity, goal clarity, team dynamics -- because the majority of underperformance traces to broken environments, not broken people.

Once conditions are genuinely sound and a manager is still contorting to make someone succeed (same feedback loop, routing work around them, tiptoeing in 1-on-1s), this is a red flag about fit, not a signal to try harder.
Continuing to prop up someone struggling in a sound environment is bad management -- it harms the team and the manager's effectiveness while deferring a necessary conversation.

The potluck metaphor extends to any domain where someone sets up conditions others opt into: communities, products, networks -- the host's job ends at the conditions and fails when it becomes personal custodianship of every participant's experience.
quotes: Your job as a leader isn't to make everyone successful. It's to create the conditions that give people the highest possible chance of success.
The host doesn't fail if someone doesn't love their neighbor's pasta salad. The host fails if they pick a spot next to a wasp nest. This might be one of the most important distinctions in management.

Before you ever blame the people, you have to make sure the conditions or the environment is sound. In my experience, a huge percentage of underperformance on teams traces back to broken environments, not broken people.

If you've done that work and you're still finding yourself contorting to make someone successful -- giving the same feedback over and over, getting defensiveness or excuses, rerouting work around them, tiptoeing in 1:1s -- that's a red flag. Not about you. About fit.
You can coach. You can support. You can clear obstacles. But you cannot do the job for them.

At some point, continuing to try is actually bad management: you're hurting the team -- and yourself -- by spending time trying to make someone who is struggling in this environment happy and successful.
